title: Say little, do much (Avot 1:15)
hook: Shammai: make study regular, say little and do much, greet everyone cheerfully

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel's three questions, ending with four famous words. Your line was care for yourself, care beyond yourself. Did you take the first small step? Today, Hillel's partner. Day two hundred forty-five.

Two guests, one party. The first says, I'll bring a little something, and walks in with a tray of food that feeds the whole room. The second promises the moon in the group chat, and shows up with a bag of ice. Today's sage is Shammai, the partner of Hillel in the chain. Later stories give him a reputation as the strict one, the one with the short temper, and you'll meet one of those stories in a few weeks. So his saying is a surprise. Because it ends with a smile.
screen: `A LITTLE SOMETHING, A WHOLE TRAY.` → `SHAMMAI, THE STRICT ONE.` → `A SAYING THAT ENDS WITH A SMILE.`

segments.voice: Shammai's saying has three parts. First: make your Torah fixed. Set a regular time for study, and keep it, instead of learning only when you happen to feel like it. Second: say little and do much. The Talmud finds the model for this in Abraham. Three strangers come to his tent in the heat of the day, and he offers them, in his words, just a morsel of bread. Then he runs to the herd for a tender calf, has cakes baked from fine flour, and brings curd and milk. He promised a snack and served a feast. The rabbis say that's how the righteous behave: they promise a little and do a lot. Third, and this is the surprise from the strict one: receive every person with a cheerful face. The Hebrew is be'sever panim yafot, literally with a pleasant, beautiful face. Every person. Not only your friends, not only the important ones. An early rabbinic collection takes it even further: give someone the best gifts in the world with a sour face, and it's as if you gave nothing; greet them warmly with empty hands, and it's as if you gave them everything. Put all three together: a steady habit, quiet follow-through, and a warm face at the door. And that closes a week of sages: judge people favorably, choose your neighbors, a question can teach a lie, half a wage, just to listen, pursue peace, care for yourself, care beyond yourself, and today, say little, do much.
screen: `MAKE YOUR STUDY FIXED.` · `A MORSEL OF BREAD, THEN A FEAST.` · `A CHEERFUL FACE FOR EVERYONE.` · `A WEEK OF SAGES.` · then, large: `SAY LITTLE, DO MUCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: warm up your face. It sounds silly. Try it anyway. Settle, and breathe. Notice what your face is doing right now. Probably nothing much, or a little tight around the eyes. Let your jaw loosen. Let your forehead go soft. Now think of the next person you'll see today, and picture greeting them the way you'd greet someone you've missed. Just hold that picture, and let the warmth reach your face. The bell holds the time.
Say little. Shammai's rule, learned from Abraham: promise a little, do a lot, and greet every person with a cheerful face.
Your line: just a morsel of bread. Today, do one kind thing without announcing it first, and greet everyone you meet with a real smile. Day two hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: A fixed daily or weekly time for Torah study, often with a study partner, is a long-standing Jewish practice, and 'receive everyone with a cheerful face' is taught as basic Jewish courtesy.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: say little and do much.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't talk too much.
what it means: promise a little, deliver a lot, keep a steady habit, and greet everyone warmly.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud draws say little, do much from Abraham, who offered a morsel of bread and served a feast.

sources.ref: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 13

notes: Abraham as the model of 'say little, do much' (and Ephron as the reverse): Bava Metzia 87a; confirm.
The teaching that a gift with a sour face is as nothing and a warm greeting with nothing is as everything: Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 13 on this mishnah; confirm the source and paraphrase.
Shammai's reputation for strictness is referenced ahead of the 'on one foot' story (Shabbat 31a), which is taught on day 272; the story is not told here.
